intro: How much fence goes around a garden? How much soil fills a planter? How many minutes until the bus comes? How heavy is the class pet this week? Every one of these questions is a measurement question. Measuring means putting a number on something real: a length, an area, a volume, a weight or a stretch of time.

In this unit you will cover shapes with squares to find area, walk around them to find perimeter, and pack boxes with cubes to find volume. Then you will change units the way a cook or a builder does, from feet to inches and from kilograms to grams. You will figure out how much time passes between two clock times.

Finally, you will turn measurements into pictures that other people can read: bar graphs, picture graphs and line plots. By the end you should be able to measure something in your own classroom, show the data on a graph, and use it to answer a question that matters to you.
bigQuestion: How do we put numbers on the space, weight and time around us, and share what we found?

timeline.t: Ancient Egyptians measure with the cubit, the length of a forearm from elbow to fingertip
Egyptian rope stretchers re-measure farm fields after each Nile flood, using knotted ropes
Euclid's Elements sets down the geometry of squares, rectangles and solids in careful proofs
Archimedes finds the volume of a sphere and compares it to the cylinder around it
Magna Carta in England calls for one standard measure for wine, ale and grain across the kingdom
William Playfair publishes some of the first bar graphs to show trade numbers as pictures
France creates the metric system, with the meter, gram and liter linked by tens
The U.S. Congress makes metric units legal to use in trade alongside feet and pounds
Seventeen nations sign the Treaty of the Meter in Paris to share one set of standards
American and Canadian railroads adopt standard time zones so every clock agrees
The United States and other nations define the inch as exactly 2.54 centimeters
The meter is redefined by how far light travels in a tiny fraction of a second

words.d: the number of unit squares that cover a flat shape, measured in square units
the distance all the way around the outside of a shape
the number of unit cubes that fill a solid shape, measured in cubic units
a rule in symbols that always works, like Area = length × width
a shape made by putting two or more simple shapes together
a box shape whose six faces are all rectangles
to change a measurement from one unit to another without changing the amount
a metric unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams
the amount of time that passes between a start time and an end time
the numbers along the side of a graph that tell what each line stands for
the note on a picture graph that says how many each picture stands for
a number line with an X stacked above each measurement, one X per time it happened

test.q: A rectangle is 6 feet by 9 feet. What is its area?
A rectangle is 6 feet by 9 feet. What is its perimeter?
Which shape has the same area as a 4 by 9 rectangle?
An L-shape is made of an 8 by 3 rectangle and a 4 by 2 rectangle. What is its area?
A box is 2 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm. What is its volume?
A box holds 40 unit cubes. Its bottom layer has 8 cubes. How tall is the box?
test.why: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 layers, so the box is 5 cubes tall.

test.q: How many inches are in 4 feet?
How many meters are in 3 kilometers?
How many cups are in 2 quarts?
test.why: Each quart is 4 cups, so 2 × 4 = 8 cups.

test.q: How many minutes are in 2 hours 15 minutes?
Art class starts at 12:40 and ends at 1:25. How long is it?
test.why: Jump 20 minutes to 1:00, then 25 minutes to 1:25. That is 45 minutes.

test.q: A bar graph has a scale of 5. A bar reaches the fourth line. What does it show?
Each apple picture stands for 2 apples. A row shows 4 and a half apples. How many apples?
test.why: 4 × 2 = 8, plus half of 2 is 1, so 9 apples.

test.q: A line plot has 2 X marks above 1/4, 3 above 1/2 and 1 above 3/4. How many measurements were made?
The same plot has X marks from 1/4 to 3/4. What is the range?

write.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 feet by 5 feet. Fence costs $4 per foot, and each bag of seed covers 10 square feet. Find how much the fence costs and how many bags of seed are needed. Explain each step and say which measurement, area or perimeter, you used for each part and why.
tips: State both answers clearly at the start: the fence cost and the number of seed bags.
Show the perimeter step with all four sides or the doubling shortcut, then multiply by the price.
Show the area step with length × width, then divide by 10 to find the bags.
Say in words why fence uses perimeter and seed uses area.
Check each answer by doing it a second way, and make sure the units say feet or square feet.
